title: 3  Classical Supervised Learning
text:
3.8 Cheat Sheet

OLS normal equations: \(\hat{\beta} = (\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{y}\) — fails when features are collinear or \(p > n\).
Ridge adds \(\lambda\mathbf{I}\) to \(\mathbf{X}^\top\mathbf{X}\), making it always invertible and shrinking coefficients.
Lasso drives coefficients to zero because the L1 ball has corners at the coordinate axes — automatic feature selection.
R² always increases with more features; use adjusted R² or out-of-sample RMSE to compare models.
VIF > 10 signals multicollinearity; affects interpretability, not prediction.
Logistic regression is a linear classifier — decision boundary is a hyperplane, not a curve.
Sigmoid output is a log-odds in linear form: \(\log(p/(1-p)) = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\).
Exponentiate logistic regression coefficients to get odds ratios: \(e^{w_j}\) = multiplicative change in odds per unit of feature \(j\).
Always use class_weight='balanced' or scale_pos_weight for imbalanced classification.
Gini ≈ entropy in practice — focus hyperparameter search on max_depth and min_samples_leaf.
Unpruned decision trees achieve 100% training accuracy — always a sign of overfitting.
Random forest feature importance is biased toward high-cardinality features — verify with permutation importance or SHAP.
OOB score ≈ cross-validation accuracy for random forests — use oob_score=True as a cheap sanity check.
Adding trees to a random forest never overfits — only increases compute and variance reduction.
Gradient boosting pseudo-residuals = negative gradient of the loss with respect to current predictions.
XGBoost uses second-order gradients (Hessian) for more accurate split gain estimates.
LightGBM is leaf-wise, XGBoost is level-wise — LightGBM is faster and often more accurate on large data.
GOSS in LightGBM: keep all high-gradient samples, subsample low-gradient samples — preserves information density.
Always use early_stopping_rounds with gradient boosting — fixed n_estimators without early stopping will overfit.
Start with learning_rate=0.05 and let early stopping find the right n_estimators; tune other params after.
SVM margin is defined by support vectors only — all other training points are irrelevant to the solution.
Large C in SVM: narrow margin, fits training data closely, risk of overfitting.
Small C in SVM: wide margin, more misclassifications allowed, more regularized.
Large gamma (RBF): each point has narrow influence — complex boundary, risk of overfitting.
SVM requires StandardScaler — without it, features with larger scales dominate the margin calculation.
LinearSVC is \(O(n)\) for text — prefer it over SVC(kernel=‘linear’) for high-dimensional sparse data.
Gradient boosting beats random forest on most tabular tasks with sufficient hyperparameter tuning.
Start with LightGBM for any new structured data problem — best default accuracy/speed tradeoff.
For interpretability under regulatory pressure: use logistic regression or decision tree, supplement with SHAP.
Rule of thumb for feature importance verification: if importance changes dramatically on retraining, you have correlated or unstable features.

title: 3  Classical Supervised Learning
text:
3.9 Interview Questions

3.9.1 Entry Level






Entry Level



Q1. What is the difference between linear regression and logistic regression?






Model Answer





Weak answer: “Linear regression predicts continuous values, logistic regression predicts classes.”
Strong answer: Linear regression models a continuous target variable as a linear combination of features: \(\hat{y} = \mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b\). It minimizes MSE and assumes the relationship between features and target is linear with normally distributed residuals. It can output any real number.
Logistic regression models the probability of a binary class label. It applies the sigmoid function to the same linear combination: \(\hat{p} = \sigma(\mathbf{w}^\top\mathbf{x} + b)\), constraining output to (0, 1). It minimizes cross-entropy loss (equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation). The decision boundary is still a hyperplane — it is a linear classifier applied to classification, not regression.
The key distinction beyond “continuous vs. discrete output” is the loss function and the meaning of the output: linear regression gives you a prediction of a quantity; logistic regression gives you a calibrated probability of class membership. Getting this nuance right is what distinguishes a candidate who understands the math from one who memorized the sklearn API.



Q2. Why do we need regularization in linear models? What’s the difference between L1 and L2?






Model Answer





Weak answer: “Regularization prevents overfitting by adding a penalty term.”
Strong answer: Regularization prevents overfitting when the model is too flexible relative to the training data — this happens when features outnumber samples, when features are correlated, or when the dataset is noisy. Both penalties shrink coefficients toward zero, reducing model complexity and variance at the cost of some bias.
L2 (Ridge) adds \(\lambda\sum\beta_j^2\) to the loss. It penalizes large coefficients by shrinking all of them proportionally, but never to exactly zero. The quadratic penalty has a smooth gradient everywhere, enabling a closed-form solution. L2 is preferred when all features are expected to contribute — it stabilizes multicollinear estimates by adding \(\lambda\mathbf{I}\) to the normal equations matrix, making it invertible.
L1 (Lasso) adds \(\lambda\sum|\beta_j|\) to the loss. The absolute value creates a non-smooth penalty at zero, which creates a mathematical incentive for the optimizer to drive coefficients exactly to zero. This produces sparse solutions — automatic feature selection. It requires coordinate descent because the gradient of \(|\beta_j|\) is undefined at zero. Preferred when you believe many features are irrelevant.
Concrete difference: run both on a dataset with 20 features, 10 of which are pure noise. Lasso will zero out roughly those 10 noise features. Ridge will shrink all 20 features but keep all non-zero.



Q3. What is the Gini impurity and how is it used in decision trees?






Model Answer





Gini impurity measures how often a randomly chosen element from a node would be incorrectly classified if it were labeled according to the class distribution in that node. Formally: \(G = 1 - \sum_k p_k^2\), where \(p_k\) is the fraction of samples in class \(k\).
At each split candidate, the decision tree computes the weighted Gini impurity of the two resulting child nodes: \(G_{split} = \frac{n_{left}}{n} G_{left} + \frac{n_{right}}{n} G_{right}\). The split that minimizes this weighted Gini (equivalently, maximizes Gini gain) is chosen. A Gini of 0 means a perfectly pure node — all one class. A Gini of 0.5 (binary classification) means maximally impure — 50/50 class distribution.
The key fact for interviews: Gini and entropy produce nearly identical results in practice. The practical differences that actually matter are tree depth controls (max_depth, min_samples_leaf), not the choice of splitting criterion.



Q4. What is bagging, and how does it improve model performance?






Model Answer





Bagging (Bootstrap Aggregating) is an ensemble technique that trains multiple instances of the same model on different bootstrap samples of the training data, then aggregates their predictions. A bootstrap sample is a random sample of the training data with replacement — the same size as the original, but with some examples appearing multiple times and others excluded.
Bagging reduces variance without increasing bias. High-variance models (like deep decision trees) give very different predictions on different training sets. By training many models on different samples and averaging their predictions, the errors from individual models cancel out — provided the errors are uncorrelated. For classification, bagging takes the majority vote; for regression, it takes the mean.
Random forests extend bagging by also randomly subsampling features at each split, which further decorrelates the individual trees and makes averaging more effective. The out-of-bag examples (the ~36.8% of samples excluded from each bootstrap) provide a free, unbiased validation estimate without a separate held-out set.



Q5. What is the kernel trick in SVMs?






Model Answer





The kernel trick allows SVMs to learn non-linear decision boundaries without ever explicitly computing the high-dimensional feature transformation.
SVMs in their dual form make predictions as: \(f(x) = \sum_i \alpha_i y_i K(x_i, x) + b\), where \(K(x_i, x) = \phi(x_i)^\top\phi(x)\) is the kernel function — the dot product in the transformed feature space. The key insight: you never need to compute \(\phi(x)\) explicitly. You only need a function \(K\) that computes the dot product in the transformed space.
For RBF: \(K(x_i, x_j) = \exp(-\gamma\|x_i - x_j\|^2)\). This corresponds to an infinite-dimensional feature space, but we compute it with a single exponential operation. The SVM can therefore learn boundaries of arbitrary smoothness without the memory cost of explicitly storing infinite-dimensional feature vectors.
Practical implication: for non-linear data, use SVC(kernel='rbf'). For text classification with TF-IDF (already high-dimensional and effectively linear), use LinearSVC — no kernel needed, dramatically faster.



Q6. When would you choose random forest over a single decision tree?






Model Answer





Almost always. A single decision tree has high variance — small changes in training data produce very different tree structures. It is prone to overfitting (an unpruned tree achieves 100% training accuracy by memorizing noise) and its accuracy is generally well below that of ensemble methods.
A random forest reduces variance dramatically by training hundreds of decorrelated trees and averaging their predictions. Individual trees still overfit, but their overfitting errors are in different directions, so they largely cancel when averaged. The random feature subsampling ensures trees disagree usefully rather than all making the same errors on the same hard examples.
The only scenario to prefer a single decision tree is when interpretability is paramount — a single tree with depth ≤ 5 can be printed, understood, and audited by non-technical stakeholders. For regulatory contexts (some credit scoring, medical decision support) where “explain every prediction” is a hard requirement, a simple decision tree may be the only option even at significant accuracy cost.



Q7. What is overfitting, and how do you detect it?






Model Answer





Overfitting occurs when a model learns the noise and idiosyncrasies of the training data so precisely that it fails to generalize to new examples. The model has high training accuracy but significantly lower validation or test accuracy.
Detection methods: (1) Train-test gap — large difference between training and test metrics (e.g., training accuracy 97%, test accuracy 72%); (2) Learning curves — plot training and validation loss vs. number of training examples; an overfit model shows low training loss and high validation loss that don’t converge; (3) Cross-validation — high variance across folds indicates the model is sensitive to which specific examples it saw; (4) Residual analysis (regression) — residuals that show systematic patterns on training data but random scatter on held-out data.
Solutions: regularization (L1/L2), reduce model complexity (fewer features, shallower trees), increase training data, use dropout (neural networks), or switch to inherently lower-variance models (e.g., random forest instead of single tree, logistic regression instead of deep polynomial regression).








3.9.2 Mid Level






Mid Level



Q1. You’re training an XGBoost model for churn prediction. Walk me through how you would set up the training pipeline, select hyperparameters, and validate the model.






Model Answer





Setup: Split data into train/validation/test (70/15/15) with stratification on the churn label. Keep the test set completely locked until final evaluation — all hyperparameter decisions use train+validation only.
Preprocessing: Handle missing values — XGBoost handles them natively, but be explicit about encoding categorical features (target encoding or enable_categorical=True). Encode the binary churn label as 0/1. Compute scale_pos_weight = (n_non_churn / n_churn) for class imbalance.
Baseline: Start with n_estimators=2000, learning_rate=0.05, early_stopping_rounds=50. Run on validation set. This gives you a solid reference point and an optimal number of rounds without tuning.
Hyperparameter search: Use Optuna or RandomizedSearchCV on a log-scale search space: max_depth in [3,8], subsample in [0.6, 1.0], colsample_bytree in [0.6, 1.0], min_child_weight in [1, 10], reg_lambda in [0.1, 10]. Use 5-fold CV with early stopping inside each fold. 50–100 trials of random/Bayesian search is sufficient.
Metrics: For churn prediction, ROC-AUC is the primary metric (model discrimination). Report also precision-recall AUC (better for imbalanced classes), and at the operating threshold: precision, recall, F1. Present the precision-recall curve to the business so they can choose the threshold that matches their cost model (cost of missed churn vs. cost of false intervention).
Validation: Final test set evaluation with the locked model. Run SHAP value analysis on test set for feature importance and model explanation. Check for data leakage (features computed using future information, e.g., last month’s support tickets when predicting this month’s churn).
Follow-up question: “How do you handle the fact that churn labels may be noisy (customers who cancelled but were actually returning seasonal users)?”
Answer: Analyze the label carefully — define churn precisely (cancelled subscription with no return in N days vs. reduced engagement). For noisy labels, use label smoothing, or treat it as a learning-with-label-noise problem. Build a holdout of “confirmed churners” with clean labels and use it as your primary evaluation set.



Q2. Explain gradient boosting. How does it differ from random forest algorithmically?






Model Answer





Random forest trains all trees in parallel on bootstrapped subsets of data. Each tree is independent — a tree at round 100 has no knowledge of what tree at round 50 learned. The ensemble reduces variance by averaging decorrelated high-variance models.
Gradient boosting trains trees sequentially, where each tree explicitly targets the errors of the current ensemble. After fitting the first tree \(F_1(x)\), compute residuals \(r_i = y_i - F_1(x_i)\). Fit the next tree \(h_2(x)\) to those residuals — not the original targets. Update \(F_2(x) = F_1(x) + \nu h_2(x)\). Repeat until convergence or early stopping.
The “gradient” in gradient boosting: for a general loss \(\mathcal{L}\), the pseudo-residuals \(r_i = -\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial F(x_i)\) are the negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current predictions. Fitting a tree to these gradients is gradient descent in function space — each tree is a step in the direction that reduces the loss fastest.
This sequential correction is why gradient boosting reduces bias (not just variance). A single tree is a high-bias model; each iteration adds a tree targeting the bias remaining. The tradeoff: overfitting risk if you run too many iterations without regularization. learning_rate scales each tree’s contribution, preventing large individual steps that overfit. early_stopping monitors validation loss to stop before overfitting begins.
Code follow-up:
# Verify gradient boosting is targeting residuals:
import lightgbm as lgb
from sklearn.datasets import make_regression
import numpy as np

X, y = make_regression(n_samples=1000, n_features=10, random_state=42)
model = lgb.LGBMRegressor(n_estimators=100, learning_rate=0.1)
model.fit(X, y)

# Predictions improve monotonically as rounds increase
staged_preds = [model.predict(X, num_iteration=i) for i in range(1, 20)]
for i, p in enumerate(staged_preds):
    print(f"Round {i+1}: MSE = {np.mean((y - p)**2):.2f}")



Q3. How does LightGBM achieve faster training than XGBoost on large datasets?






Model Answer





Three innovations work together:
1. Leaf-wise vs. level-wise growth. XGBoost expands all nodes at a given depth level before going deeper — breadth-first. LightGBM always expands the single leaf with the highest loss reduction — best-first. For a fixed number of leaves, leaf-wise typically produces lower loss because it focuses capacity where it matters most. Fewer leaves are wasted on low-gain splits.
2. GOSS (Gradient-based One-Side Sampling). Training examples with small gradient magnitude contribute little to the tree-building objective — the model already explains them well. LightGBM keeps all high-gradient instances (the “hard” examples) and randomly downsamples low-gradient instances. With weights to compensate for the downsampling, this gives nearly identical split gain estimates using a fraction of the data. On a 10 million row dataset, this can reduce effective training data by 80% with minimal accuracy loss.
3. EFB (Exclusive Feature Bundling). In one-hot-encoded or sparse data, many features are mutually exclusive (only one is non-zero at a time). EFB identifies these bundles and creates a single dense feature encoding the bundle, reducing feature count from thousands to hundreds without information loss.
Practical upshot: On 1M rows with 200 features, LightGBM typically trains 5-10x faster than XGBoost at comparable accuracy. For less than 10k rows, both are fast enough that the difference is irrelevant — focus on accuracy hyperparameters instead.
When to prefer XGBoost: Exact split finding (not histogram-based) is XGBoost’s default and can be marginally more accurate on very small datasets. Also, XGBoost’s GPU implementation (tree_method='gpu_hist') is more mature.



Q4. You have a random forest model in production. After retraining on new data, the top feature importances changed dramatically. What do you investigate?






Model Answer





This is a common production debugging scenario. I’d investigate in this order:
1. Feature correlation: If two correlated features (A and B) were both important, the forest may switch which one it uses as the primary splitter depending on small changes in training data. MDI importance splits credit between correlated features arbitrarily. Check if the new “top features” are correlated with the old ones — correlation doesn’t mean the model is wrong, just that importance is distributed differently between correlated signals.
2. Data distribution shift: Did the new training data have a different distribution? Plot the feature distributions (histograms, quantiles) for old vs new training data. If a previously important feature now has near-zero variance in the new data, it will correctly appear less important.
3. Target distribution shift: Did the base rate or the relationships between features and target change? This is especially common in fraud, ad click, and financial data. Plot feature-target correlations across time.
4. Data leakage or preprocessing bug: Did a new feature get added that leaks the target? A feature with unrealistically high importance on training but poor test performance is a leakage red flag.
5. Random seed / bootstrap variance: Rerun training multiple times with different seeds. If importance rankings are highly variable across seeds, your features may be weakly informative and bootstrapping is capturing noise. Use more trees (n_estimators > 500) to stabilize estimates.
Final check: Compare MDI importance vs. permutation importance on a held-out test set. If permutation importance shows a different pattern than MDI, permutation importance is more reliable.



Q5. When would you use SVM over gradient boosting for a classification problem?






Model Answer





Practical cases where I’d consider SVM:
1. Small, high-dimensional data (n << p): Gene expression datasets (\(n\) = 200 patients, \(p\) = 10,000 genes), NLP before transformers with TF-IDF features. SVMs have tight generalization bounds in this regime; gradient boosting will overfit or build trees on noise features.
2. Sparse feature spaces: Text classification with bag-of-words or TF-IDF. LinearSVC is extremely fast on sparse matrices via liblinear. XGBoost and LightGBM handle sparse data but are not as natively optimized for bag-of-words input.
3. When you have domain-specific kernels: If you can define a meaningful similarity function between samples (molecular fingerprints, protein sequences, graph structures), SVMs can directly use that similarity as a kernel. Gradient boosting requires you to engineer explicit features.
In practice: I would always run a logistic regression baseline first. If logistic regression and gradient boosting are already close in accuracy, adding SVM rarely improves things enough to justify the slower hyperparameter tuning. SVMs are not in my default go-to set for tabular data with \(n > 50{,}000\).



Q6. How do you handle class imbalance in a binary classifier? Walk through multiple strategies.






Model Answer





Understand the problem first. Is the imbalance reflecting the real-world distribution (e.g., fraud is genuinely rare)? Then you want a model calibrated to that distribution — don’t resample to 50/50 and then apply that model to a world that is 0.1% positive.
Strategy 1 — Cost-sensitive learning. Most algorithms support class_weight='balanced' or scale_pos_weight. This upweights minority class errors in the loss function. For gradient boosting: scale_pos_weight = n_negative / n_positive. Clean, no data modification, generally the first thing to try.
Strategy 2 — Threshold adjustment. Train on the true distribution, then shift the decision threshold from 0.5 to match your cost model. If missing a positive costs 10x more than a false positive, you want higher recall even at precision cost. Plot precision-recall curve, pick the operating point that matches the business tradeoff.
Strategy 3 — Oversampling (SMOTE). Synthesize new minority class samples by interpolating between existing minority samples in feature space. Reduces overfitting vs naive duplication. Use imbalanced-learn library. Caution: always apply SMOTE inside the cross-validation fold (fit on training fold, evaluate on untouched validation fold).
Strategy 4 — Undersampling. Randomly remove majority class samples. Loses information — only useful when dataset is very large and you can afford to discard majority examples.
Strategy 5 — Anomaly detection framing. For extreme imbalance (1:10,000+), consider framing as anomaly detection: train an isolation forest or autoencoder on majority class, flag minority class as anomalies. No positive labels needed.
Metric choice: Accuracy is useless with severe imbalance. Use ROC-AUC for discrimination ability, PR-AUC for precision-recall tradeoff, and F1 or F-beta (with beta weighting precision vs recall per your business case) for binary decisions.








3.9.3 Senior Level






Senior Level



Q1. Walk me through how XGBoost builds trees differently from a random forest. Be precise.






Model Answer






🎯 What great looks like: A senior candidate explains both the algorithmic differences and the practical implications — when each wins, and why. They mention second-order gradients and regularized objectives, not just “sequential vs parallel.”

Random forest builds \(T\) independent trees, each on a bootstrapped sample of data, each considering \(\sqrt{p}\) features per split. Trees are fully grown (or pruned with hyperparameters). Predictions are averaged. The goal is reducing variance through decorrelated aggregation.
XGBoost builds trees sequentially. At round \(m\), it computes the gradient \(g_i = \partial \mathcal{L}/\partial \hat{y}_i^{(m-1)}\) and Hessian \(h_i = \partial^2 \mathcal{L}/\partial (\hat{y}_i^{(m-1)})^2\) of the loss for every training example. The new tree is fit to minimize the second-order Taylor approximation of the total loss:
\[\mathcal{L}^{(m)} \approx \sum_i [g_i f_m(x_i) + \frac{1}{2}h_i f_m^2(x_i)] + \gamma T + \frac{1}{2}\lambda\sum_j w_j^2\]
For each candidate split, XGBoost computes the exact gain analytically: \(\text{Gain} = \frac{1}{2}\left[\frac{G_L^2}{H_L + \lambda} + \frac{G_R^2}{H_R + \lambda} - \frac{(G_L+G_R)^2}{H_L+H_R+\lambda}\right] - \gamma\). If gain \(< 0\), the split is pruned immediately. This is fundamentally different from random forest splitting criteria — XGBoost evaluates each split against a regularized objective rather than raw impurity.
The Hessian \(h_i\) weights each sample’s contribution to split gain. For squared loss, \(h_i = 1\) (all samples equal weight). For log-loss (classification), \(h_i = \hat{p}_i(1-\hat{p}_i)\) — samples near the decision boundary (uncertainty) get higher weight in split selection. This is why XGBoost often builds more accurate boundaries near the decision surface.
Practical difference: XGBoost reduces bias through sequential correction; random forest reduces variance through averaging. On most tabular tasks, bias reduction wins — XGBoost outperforms. But random forest is more stable with minimal tuning and harder to overfit.

⚠️ Common Mistake: Saying XGBoost is “just boosted trees” without explaining the second-order approximation and regularized objective. That’s the core innovation that separates XGBoost from earlier gradient boosting implementations like sklearn’s GradientBoostingClassifier.




Q2. You have 100k samples and 500 features. Which model do you start with and why?






Model Answer






🎯 What great looks like: A senior candidate answers with a decision process, not a single algorithm. They identify that the answer depends on the target variable type, feature characteristics, and business requirements — then commit to a concrete recommendation.

My default starting point: LightGBM. At 100k samples and 500 features, this is the sweet spot where gradient boosting consistently outperforms. My reasoning:
Why not start with simpler models: Logistic/linear regression would require significant feature engineering (handling non-linearity, interactions) and would struggle with 500 potentially correlated features without careful regularization. A random forest would give a decent baseline but consistently loses to gradient boosting with even modest tuning.
Why LightGBM specifically: 100k rows with 500 features trains in under 60 seconds. Built-in handling of missing values. Native categorical support (enable_categorical=True) avoids one-hot explosion. GOSS and EFB work well at this scale. early_stopping_rounds gives automatic convergence. I can have a solid baseline in under 2 hours including feature importance analysis.
Feature assessment first: With 500 features, I’d first check: - Are any features high-cardinality IDs? Drop them or target-encode. - Are features sparse (many zeros)? LightGBM handles this well. - Are features correlated (VIF)? LightGBM’s column subsampling handles this; I’ll also run permutation importance to surface correlated redundancy. - Missing value percentage per feature? LightGBM handles natively; document the pattern.
First LightGBM run setup:
model = lgb.LGBMClassifier(
    n_estimators=5000,
    learning_rate=0.05,
    num_leaves=63,
    min_data_in_leaf=20,
    feature_fraction=0.8,
    bagging_fraction=0.8,
    bagging_freq=5,
    is_unbalance=True,  # if imbalanced
    n_jobs=-1
)
model.fit(X_train, y_train,
          eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)],
          callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(100), lgb.log_evaluation(200)])
Exceptions that change the answer: - If interpretability is a hard requirement → start with logistic regression, explain why gradient boosting doesn’t meet that constraint - If inference must be <1ms → LightGBM is still fine, but test before committing - If many features are text/images → LightGBM is not the right tool; need neural approach

⚠️ Common Mistake: Starting with neural networks on a structured tabular dataset of this size. Every Kaggle structured data competition with a tree ensemble winner demonstrates that gradient boosting systematically beats MLPs on tabular data without extensive architecture tuning. Neural networks win on images, text, and sequences — not flat feature vectors.




Q3. Your Random Forest feature importances changed dramatically after retraining on new data. What’s happening and how do you debug it?






Model Answer






🎯 What great looks like: Systematic root-cause analysis covering both algorithmic properties of RF importances and data/production issues. Shows understanding of MDI bias and proposes actionable diagnostic steps.

Step 1: Understand that this can be normal. MDI (impurity-based) importance is a property of this specific trained forest on this specific data. Correlated features will arbitrarily distribute credit between them based on which ones happen to be sampled at the top splits. With 500 features and significant correlation, large swings in individual feature rankings are expected even with identical underlying data.
Step 2: Quantify the change. Is the top-5 list completely different, or just reshuffled within a correlated group? If “square footage” and “number of rooms” swap positions, that’s expected. If “user_id” suddenly became the top feature when it wasn’t before, that’s a bug.
Step 3: Check for data issues. - New feature added to data pipeline that leaks the target? A feature with 99% importance is almost certainly leakage. - Distribution shift in an important feature? If “transaction amount” now has a different scale or encoding, its importance changes. - Sample size change affecting which features have enough signal? - Train/test split change causing a different feature to capture temporal leakage?
Step 4: Cross-validate the importances. Train 5 forests on 5 different subsamples and plot importance distributions. If a feature’s importance has high variance across folds, it’s borderline — not reliably important. If importances are stable across folds but different from before, the data genuinely changed.
Step 5: Switch to permutation importance. Run permutation importance on a held-out test set for both the old and new model. This is less sensitive to data-specific split artifacts and gives you a more stable signal. If permutation importance also changed dramatically, the feature-target relationships themselves changed (distribution shift).
Step 6: SHAP analysis. SHAP values decompose each prediction into per-feature contributions. Comparing SHAP distributions for old vs new model data reveals whether specific subpopulations changed, not just aggregate importances.

⚠️ Common Mistake: Treating importance changes as always indicating a problem. Sometimes it just means correlated features switched which one happened to be chosen for the top splits. The model’s predictions may be equally accurate.




Q4. Design a production fraud detection system. Walk through model selection, training, and deployment.






Model Answer






🎯 What great looks like: Treats this as a system design problem, not just a modeling problem. Addresses: label quality, class imbalance, temporal validation, feature engineering, model serving, monitoring, feedback loops.

Problem framing: Binary classification — transaction is fraud (1) or not (0). Severe class imbalance (~0.1% fraud rate). Time-ordered data — temporal leakage is the biggest trap. Latency constraint: real-time decision (<100ms) or async review (<1 second)?
Data and labels: - Labels have lag: fraud is often confirmed days after transaction (chargebacks, investigations). Don’t train on transactions with labels still uncertain. Use confirmed labels only, with a cutoff. - Label noise: some fraud goes undetected (false negatives in training data). Accept this — don’t over-engineer against it. - Temporal split: train on T to T+12 months, validate on T+12 to T+15, test on T+15 to T+18. Never shuffle and split randomly — this leaks future patterns into training.
Feature engineering: - Transaction features: amount, merchant category, time of day, device, location - Velocity features: transactions in past 1h, 24h, 7d per card/user/device (window aggregations) - Behavioral deviation: is this amount/merchant unusual for this user? - Network features: is this card/account linked to known fraud patterns? - These window features require a feature store for low-latency serving.
Model selection: - Start with LightGBM. Handles class imbalance with is_unbalance=True. Fast inference (microseconds). Feature importance + SHAP for explainability. - Consider a stacking ensemble: LightGBM + logistic regression on LightGBM leaf indices (a classic Kaggle technique that often gives +1-2% AUC). - Neural networks (tabular DNN) can capture feature interactions LightGBM misses, but require more engineering. Worth A/B testing after LightGBM is in production.
Validation: - Primary metric: ROC-AUC and PR-AUC (both matter for imbalanced data) - At operating threshold: precision, recall, F-beta (tune beta to match cost model: missed fraud cost vs false alarm cost) - Evaluate on temporal holdout — not random split - Check performance stratified by transaction type, merchant category, geography — ensure model is fair and consistent
Deployment: - Model served via low-latency endpoint (FastAPI + model binary, or ONNX for cross-platform serving) - Feature store provides pre-computed window aggregations at <10ms - Decision is synchronous for card-present transactions; can be async for card-not-present - Model output is a probability → business rule layer applies thresholds (block/review/pass)
Monitoring: - PSI (Population Stability Index) on input features: detects distribution shift before model degrades - Model performance: precision/recall on confirmed fraud labels (with label lag — report with proper accounting for this) - Score distribution monitoring: if average fraud probability changes significantly without business cause, something is wrong - Data pipeline freshness: if feature store is stale, model performance degrades silently
Retraining: - Monthly scheduled retraining on rolling 12-month window - Champion-challenger A/B testing for new model versions - Trigger: PSI > 0.25 on any important feature, or recall drops below threshold on validation window

⚠️ Common Mistake: Building a model without accounting for temporal leakage in the validation split. Shuffling transaction data and doing 80/20 split will give artificially high CV performance because future patterns leak into training. Real performance will be significantly worse.




Q5. How do you handle severe class imbalance (1:1000) in a fraud detection model? What if standard techniques fail?






Model Answer






🎯 What great looks like: Goes beyond SMOTE/class_weight. Addresses why naive approaches fail at 1:1000, and proposes anomaly detection, cost-sensitive learning, and threshold calibration as a coherent system.

Why standard approaches fail at 1:1000: With only 0.1% positive rate, SMOTE generates synthetic minority samples in a sparse region with few real examples — the interpolations may not reflect real fraud patterns. Naive oversampling causes overfitting to specific fraud patterns and poor generalization to new attack vectors.
Tier 1 — Always do this first: - scale_pos_weight = 1000 in LightGBM/XGBoost — free, no data modification - Evaluate with PR-AUC, not ROC-AUC. ROC-AUC can be misleadingly high with severe imbalance; PR-AUC directly measures precision-recall tradeoff on the positive class. - Set decision threshold based on business cost model, not 0.5.
Tier 2 — If Tier 1 is insufficient: - Focal loss: A modification of cross-entropy that down-weights easy-to-classify majority examples during training, focusing learning signal on hard examples near the decision boundary. alpha controls class weighting, gamma controls hard example focus. - Isotonic regression calibration on validation set to ensure predicted probabilities are accurate — critical when downstream decisions depend on the probability value.
Tier 3 — Architectural approaches: - Anomaly detection pre-filter: Train an autoencoder or Isolation Forest on majority class (normal transactions). Flag transactions with high reconstruction error as candidate fraud. Use this as a binary feature in the main model, or as a two-stage pipeline (anomaly score > threshold → expensive model review). - Two-stage pipeline: Fast first stage (logistic regression or rule-based) to filter obvious legitimate transactions. Second stage runs detailed model only on flagged transactions. Reduces effective imbalance at second stage. - Contrastive learning / self-supervised pre-training: Pretrain a representation on the majority class (normal transactions), then fine-tune with few fraud examples. Similar to how few-shot learning works.
Tier 4 — Data acquisition: - The real fix for severe imbalance is more labels. If you have 1 million transactions and 1000 frauds, consider: active learning (have human analysts label uncertain predictions), semi-supervised learning (use unlabeled examples to improve representations), or partnerships with industry groups for shared fraud labels.
Failure mode to watch for: If the model achieves high PR-AUC in offline evaluation but underperforms in production, the fraud distribution has shifted (new attack vectors). Monitor precision on confirmed catches — if precision drops without recall dropping, the model is being exploited by new patterns.

⚠️ Common Mistake: Reporting accuracy as a metric. With 1:1000 imbalance, predicting “not fraud” for everything gives 99.9% accuracy. Accuracy is meaningless here. Always use PR-AUC, recall at fixed precision, or F-beta as primary metrics.




Q6. A logistic regression and a gradient boosting model have the same ROC-AUC on your test set, but you must choose one for production. How do you decide?






Model Answer






🎯 What great looks like: Recognizes that equal accuracy doesn’t mean equal appropriateness for production. Considers latency, interpretability, maintenance overhead, calibration, and failure modes.

Questions I ask before deciding:
1. Latency requirements. Logistic regression inference is a dot product — nanoseconds. Gradient boosting is hundreds of tree traversals — microseconds to low milliseconds. Both are fine for batch; for real-time with <1ms SLA, logistic regression wins.
2. Interpretability requirements. Regulatory contexts (GDPR Article 22, ECOA in US credit) require explainable decisions. Logistic regression provides direct coefficient interpretation as log-odds. Gradient boosting requires SHAP values — accurate but adds infrastructure complexity. If “why was this loan denied” must be answered, logistic regression has a significant operational advantage.
3. Probability calibration. Logistic regression outputs well-calibrated probabilities by construction (under correct model specification). Gradient boosting is typically well-calibrated but should be checked with a calibration curve. If downstream decisions rely on precise probabilities (e.g., expected loss = probability × amount), calibration matters.
4. Maintenance overhead. Logistic regression degrades gracefully with distribution shift — its coefficients have clear interpretations and it’s easy to retrain quickly. Gradient boosting requires more careful hyperparameter tuning on each retrain and its feature importance analysis is more complex.
5. Failure mode analysis. What happens when each model is wrong? Gradient boosting may capture complex interactions that logistic regression misses — but it may also capture spurious interactions that break with distribution shift. Logistic regression’s simplicity is also its robustness.
My default recommendation: If equal AUC is measured on a properly held-out test set (not just CV), choose gradient boosting for prediction-focused systems where accuracy in 6 months matters. Choose logistic regression for regulatory or interpretability-constrained systems, or for systems with aggressive latency or maintenance budgets.
But investigate first: Are they truly equal? Run a calibration curve, check performance on stratified subgroups (not just overall AUC), and verify on a time-forward holdout (not a random split). “Equal AUC on random test set” does not always mean “equal performance in production over time.”

⚠️ Common Mistake: Defaulting to the more complex model because it “feels better” or is more technically impressive. Production ML is engineering. If logistic regression meets the requirements, it’s often the correct choice.




Q7. Explain the bias-variance tradeoff. How does it manifest differently in decision trees, random forests, and gradient boosting?






Model Answer






🎯 What great looks like: Goes beyond the textbook definition. Explains how each algorithm controls the tradeoff mechanically, and connects it to hyperparameter choices.

The tradeoff: Total expected prediction error = Bias² + Variance + Irreducible noise. - Bias: Error from wrong assumptions (underfitting) — model is too simple to capture the true relationship - Variance: Error from sensitivity to training data (overfitting) — model captures noise rather than signal - You cannot simultaneously minimize both with a fixed model class
Decision trees: - Shallow tree: high bias (misses complex patterns), low variance (stable across different training samples) - Deep unpruned tree: zero bias (memorizes training data), high variance (completely unstable — different training samples produce entirely different trees) - max_depth directly controls this tradeoff. Hyperparameter selection is entirely about bias-variance balance.
Random forests: - Each tree: low bias (fully grown), high variance - Averaging \(T\) uncorrelated trees: variance reduces by factor \(T\) (theoretically), bias stays the same - RF primarily attacks variance, not bias. This is why RF can’t outperform a single decision tree on the same training data — it gives up some accuracy there — but generalizes much better. - max_features controls tree correlation; n_estimators controls variance reduction ceiling.
Gradient boosting: - Each tree: high bias (shallow), low variance (weak learner) - Sequential addition: each tree reduces the bias of the ensemble (targets remaining errors) - More rounds → lower bias, but also potentially higher variance (overfitting) - n_estimators controls bias; learning_rate, max_depth, subsample control overfitting (variance) - This is why gradient boosting often outperforms random forest: it reduces both bias and variance when properly regularized, whereas RF can only reduce variance.
Practical implication: When a random forest is underfitting (training accuracy low), you typically cannot fix it — the model class has limited capacity. When gradient boosting is underfitting, increase n_estimators or max_depth. When either is overfitting, random forest is more robust (just stop adding trees early); gradient boosting requires careful learning_rate + early stopping discipline.

title: 4  Unsupervised Learning, Evaluation Metrics & Feature Engineering
text:
5 Section 1: Unsupervised Learning
Unsupervised learning is the problem of finding structure in data without labels. The two dominant sub-problems are clustering (grouping similar instances together) and dimensionality reduction (projecting high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional space while preserving meaningful structure). Both appear constantly in production ML pipelines — clustering for customer segmentation, anomaly detection, and preprocessing; dimensionality reduction for visualization, feature compression, and noise removal.
The practical challenge with unsupervised methods is that “correct” is not well-defined — you have no labels to evaluate against. This pushes you toward domain knowledge, internal metrics, and downstream task performance as your judges. This ambiguity is intentional in interview questions: if you say “I’d evaluate the clustering using accuracy,” that is a red flag.

title: 4  Unsupervised Learning, Evaluation Metrics & Feature Engineering
text:
5.1 Clustering

5.1.1 K-Means
Plain-English definition: Partition n data points into k clusters by iteratively assigning each point to its nearest centroid and recomputing centroids until convergence.
How it works: K-Means is a coordinate descent algorithm minimizing within-cluster sum of squared distances (WCSS). The standard algorithm (Lloyd’s algorithm) operates in three steps:

Initialize k centroids — randomly or using k-means++ (smarter seeding that spreads initial centroids out to reduce pathological initializations)
Assignment step: assign each point to the nearest centroid by Euclidean distance
Update step: recompute each centroid as the mean of all points assigned to it
Repeat steps 2 and 3 until centroid positions change by less than a tolerance threshold (convergence)

The algorithm guarantees convergence but only to a local minimum of WCSS, not the global minimum. The quality of the solution depends heavily on initialization. K-means++ initialization reduces the probability of poor solutions by selecting subsequent centroids with probability proportional to their squared distance from the nearest existing centroid — this typically produces 2-5× better solutions than random initialization with negligible additional cost.
Choosing k — elbow method and silhouette score: Neither method tells you the “true” k. The elbow method plots WCSS against k; the point where the marginal decrease in WCSS stops being dramatic is the “elbow.” In practice, the elbow is often ambiguous. The silhouette score for a point measures how similar it is to its own cluster versus the next nearest cluster: \(s = (b - a) / \max(a, b)\) where \(a\) is the mean intra-cluster distance and \(b\) is the mean distance to the nearest other cluster. Silhouette ranges from -1 to +1; values above 0.5 indicate dense, well-separated clusters.






Warning



Common Mistake: Using only the elbow method to choose k. The elbow is often a bend, not a clean inflection point. Always pair it with silhouette scores, and validate the final cluster count against domain knowledge. A marketing team might have business reasons why k=4 matters even if k=6 scores slightly better.


Limitations:

Assumes spherical, equally-sized clusters — fails on elongated, irregular, or varying-density clusters
Sensitive to outliers: a single outlier can pull a centroid significantly
Requires specifying k upfront — a parameter that often requires domain knowledge you may not have
Does not handle non-convex cluster shapes (two interlocking crescents, for example)
Scales well (O(n·k·i·d) per iteration, where i = iterations, d = dimensions) but degrades in very high dimensions due to the curse of dimensionality flattening distance distributions

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.metrics import silhouette_score
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Always scale before clustering — K-Means is distance-based
X = StandardScaler().fit_transform(data)

# Elbow method + silhouette
inertias, silhouettes = [], []
K_range = range(2, 11)

for k in K_range:
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, init='k-means++', n_init=10, random_state=42)
    labels = km.fit_predict(X)
    inertias.append(km.inertia_)
    silhouettes.append(silhouette_score(X, labels))

# Plot both together to cross-validate k choice
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))
ax1.plot(K_range, inertias, 'bo-')
ax1.set_xlabel('k'); ax1.set_ylabel('WCSS (inertia)'); ax1.set_title('Elbow Method')
ax2.plot(K_range, silhouettes, 'rs-')
ax2.set_xlabel('k'); ax2.set_ylabel('Silhouette Score'); ax2.set_title('Silhouette Score')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

💡 Senior Tip: In production, K-Means cluster labels shift between runs unless you pin random_state. If your pipeline relies on cluster IDs being stable (e.g., “cluster 2 = high-value customers”), use label alignment or assign semantic labels post-hoc rather than depending on raw cluster indices.




5.1.2 DBSCAN
Plain-English definition: Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise — group points that are tightly packed together and label points in sparse regions as noise, without needing to specify the number of clusters.
How it works: DBSCAN classifies each point as one of three types:

Core point: has at least min_samples other points within radius epsilon (its neighborhood is dense enough)
Border point: within epsilon of a core point but has fewer than min_samples in its own neighborhood
Noise point: neither core nor border — isolated point in a sparse region

Clusters are formed by connecting core points within epsilon of each other (transitively), with border points assigned to the cluster of their nearest core point. This naturally handles arbitrary cluster shapes — any connected region of sufficient density becomes a cluster, regardless of its shape.
Hyperparameter intuition: epsilon sets the neighborhood radius — think of it as “how close is ‘nearby’?” min_samples sets the density threshold — how many neighbors are required to call a region dense. A starting heuristic: set min_samples to 2×dimensions (at minimum), then use a k-distance plot (sort distances to the min_samples-th nearest neighbor) to identify the “knee” as a good epsilon.






Warning



Common Mistake: Running DBSCAN on unscaled features. If one feature has range 0-1000 and another has range 0-1, the large-scale feature dominates the distance calculation entirely. Always scale features to the same range before running any distance-based algorithm.


When to use: - Data has clusters of irregular, non-convex shapes - You have outliers and want them explicitly identified (noise points) - You do not know k in advance - Spatial data (geolocation, sensor data)
When NOT to use: - Clusters have very different densities (DBSCAN uses a single epsilon across all clusters — it will merge sparse clusters or split dense ones) - Very high-dimensional data (all distance-based methods suffer here) - You need exactly k clusters for a downstream system
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN
from sklearn.neighbors import NearestNeighbors

# Find good epsilon with k-distance plot
k = 2 * X.shape[1]  # heuristic: 2 * n_features
nbrs = NearestNeighbors(n_neighbors=k).fit(X)
distances, _ = nbrs.kneighbors(X)
distances = np.sort(distances[:, -1])  # distance to k-th nearest neighbor

plt.plot(distances)
plt.xlabel('Points (sorted)'); plt.ylabel(f'{k}-NN distance')
plt.title('K-Distance Plot — knee = good epsilon')
plt.show()

# Fit DBSCAN
db = DBSCAN(eps=0.5, min_samples=k)
labels = db.fit_predict(X)

n_clusters = len(set(labels)) - (1 if -1 in labels else 0)
n_noise = (labels == -1).sum()
print(f"Clusters: {n_clusters}, Noise points: {n_noise} ({100*n_noise/len(labels):.1f}%)")

💡 Senior Tip: In fraud detection and anomaly detection pipelines, the noise points (-1 labels) from DBSCAN are often the most interesting output — they are the anomalies. The cluster labels may be less important than the outlier flags.




5.1.3 Hierarchical Clustering
Plain-English definition: Build a tree of clusters either bottom-up (agglomerative — start with each point as its own cluster and merge the most similar pair) or top-down (divisive — start with one cluster and recursively split it).
Agglomerative clustering (overwhelmingly more common in practice) uses a linkage criterion to define the distance between two clusters (as opposed to two points):

Single linkage: distance = minimum pairwise distance between any point in cluster A and any point in cluster B. Prone to “chaining” — creates long, stretched clusters because one close pair merges two clusters.
Complete linkage: distance = maximum pairwise distance. Produces more compact, spherical clusters. Sensitive to outliers.
Average linkage: distance = average of all pairwise distances. More robust than single or complete.
Ward linkage: merge the two clusters that minimize the increase in total within-cluster variance. Tends to produce equally-sized, compact clusters. This is usually the default choice.

The dendrogram is a tree diagram showing the merge order and merge distances. The height of each merge branch represents how dissimilar the merged clusters were. To cut the dendrogram into k clusters, draw a horizontal line at the appropriate height. The advantage is that you can defer the choice of k until after fitting — you fit once and explore multiple k values by changing the cut height.
When to use: - You want to explore the data’s hierarchical structure without committing to a k upfront - Small to medium datasets (hierarchical clustering is O(n²) to O(n³) and does not scale to millions of points) - Domain requires interpretable merge hierarchies (e.g., phylogenetic trees, document taxonomy)
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import dendrogram, linkage, fcluster
from scipy.spatial.distance import pdist

# Compute linkage matrix — 'ward' is almost always the right default
Z = linkage(X, method='ward')

# Visualize
plt.figure(figsize=(12, 5))
dendrogram(Z, truncate_mode='lastp', p=30, leaf_font_size=10)
plt.title('Hierarchical Clustering Dendrogram (Ward linkage)')
plt.xlabel('Sample index or cluster size'); plt.ylabel('Distance')
plt.show()

# Cut the tree at desired number of clusters
k = 4
labels = fcluster(Z, k, criterion='maxclust')



5.1.4 Gaussian Mixture Models (GMM)
Plain-English definition: Model the data as a weighted sum of k Gaussian distributions. Each point gets a probability of belonging to each cluster (soft clustering), unlike K-Means where assignment is hard (binary).
How it works: A GMM assumes data is generated from k Gaussian components, each with its own mean \(\mu_k\), covariance matrix \(\Sigma_k\), and mixture weight \(\pi_k\) (summing to 1). Fitting a GMM means learning these parameters to maximize the likelihood of the observed data. Because each point’s cluster assignment is a latent (hidden) variable, this is solved with the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm:

E-step: Given current parameters, compute the posterior probability that each point was generated by each component (responsibilities)
M-step: Update parameters (means, covariances, weights) to maximize expected log-likelihood given those responsibilities
Repeat until log-likelihood converges

Relation to K-Means: K-Means is a special case of GMM where all covariance matrices are constrained to \(\epsilon I\) (spherical, equal-sized) and assignments are hard (argmax instead of soft probabilities). GMMs are strictly more expressive. The covariance structure can be parameterized in several ways: full (each cluster has its own arbitrary covariance), tied (all share one covariance), diag (diagonal covariance only), spherical (scalar variance only).
When to use: - You want soft cluster membership (probabilities, not just labels) — useful when a customer could plausibly belong to two segments - Clusters are elliptical rather than spherical — full covariance handles this - You want a generative model: you can sample new data points from a fitted GMM






Warning



Common Mistake: Choosing full covariance on small datasets or high-dimensional data. Full covariance matrices have O(d²) parameters per component. With d=100 features and k=5 clusters, that is 50,000 covariance parameters to estimate from your data. Use diag or tied when data is limited relative to dimensionality.


from sklearn.mixture import GaussianMixture
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# Select number of components using BIC (Bayesian Information Criterion)
# Lower BIC = better fit penalized for complexity
bic_scores = []
K_range = range(1, 11)
for k in K_range:
    gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=k, covariance_type='full',
                          n_init=5, random_state=42)
    gmm.fit(X)
    bic_scores.append(gmm.bic(X))

best_k = K_range[np.argmin(bic_scores)]
print(f"Best k by BIC: {best_k}")

# Fit final model
gmm = GaussianMixture(n_components=best_k, covariance_type='full',
                      n_init=10, random_state=42)
gmm.fit(X)

# Soft assignments: each row sums to 1
responsibilities = gmm.predict_proba(X)
# Hard assignments
hard_labels = gmm.predict(X)

title: 4  Unsupervised Learning, Evaluation Metrics & Feature Engineering
text:
5.2 Dimensionality Reduction

5.2.1 PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
Plain-English definition: Find the directions (principal components) along which the data varies most, and project the data onto those directions to get a lower-dimensional representation.
How it works: PCA finds an orthogonal basis for the data by computing the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix. The eigenvector with the largest eigenvalue is the direction of maximum variance (first principal component), the second eigenvector (orthogonal to the first) captures the second-most variance, and so on. Projecting the data onto the top-k eigenvectors reduces dimensionality from d to k while retaining the most variance possible.
The eigenvectors are computed via singular value decomposition (SVD) of the centered data matrix rather than explicitly constructing the covariance matrix — this is numerically more stable and efficient. The proportion of variance explained by each component is its eigenvalue divided by the sum of all eigenvalues. A scree plot plots the cumulative variance explained vs. number of components; the “elbow” suggests how many components to retain.
When to use: - Preprocessing before a distance-sensitive algorithm (K-Means, K-NN, SVM) on high-dimensional data - Removing noise from data (lower components often capture noise rather than signal) - Computational speedup: replace 500 features with 20 PCA components before training - Visualization (project to 2D or 3D, though t-SNE/UMAP is better for this)
Limitations: - Strictly linear: cannot capture non-linear structure (two interlocking spirals would not be separated) - Principal components are linear combinations of original features — not directly interpretable - Sensitive to feature scale — always standardize before PCA - Information loss is inevitable: unless you retain all components, some variance is discarded






Warning



Common Mistake: Fitting PCA on the full dataset (including the test set) before splitting. This leaks information about the test set into the transformation. Always fit PCA on the training set only and apply the learned transformation to the test set.


from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

# Scale first — PCA is variance-based, scale affects variance
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_train)
X_test_scaled = scaler.transform(X_test)  # note: transform, not fit_transform

# Fit PCA — keep enough components to explain 95% of variance
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95, random_state=42)  # float = variance threshold
X_pca = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)

print(f"Reduced from {X_scaled.shape[1]} to {X_pca.shape[1]} components")
print(f"Variance explained: {pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum():.3f}")

# Scree plot
cumvar = np.cumsum(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)
plt.plot(range(1, len(cumvar)+1), cumvar, 'o-')
plt.axhline(0.95, color='r', linestyle='--', label='95% threshold')
plt.xlabel('Number of components'); plt.ylabel('Cumulative variance explained')
plt.legend(); plt.title('PCA Scree Plot'); plt.show()

# Apply same transformation to test set
X_test_pca = pca.transform(X_test_scaled)



5.2.2 t-SNE (t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding)
Plain-English definition: A non-linear dimensionality reduction technique that places similar high-dimensional points close together in a 2D or 3D map, optimized for visualization.
How it works: t-SNE converts pairwise distances in high-dimensional space into probabilities (high probability = nearby points), does the same in the low-dimensional space using a Student-t distribution (heavier tails than Gaussian — this prevents crowding), and minimizes the KL divergence between the two probability distributions via gradient descent. The result is a 2D or 3D embedding where local neighborhoods are preserved: points that were close in the original space cluster together in the plot.
The perplexity hyperparameter controls the effective number of local neighbors considered for each point. Perplexity between 5 and 50 is typical; lower = more local structure preserved, higher = more global structure. Results are sensitive to perplexity and run-to-run variability (the optimization is non-convex).
Critical limitations — this is where candidates frequently lose points: - t-SNE is not deterministic by default: different random seeds produce different-looking plots. This is not a bug, but it means you cannot compare two separate t-SNE runs directly. - The distances between clusters in a t-SNE plot are not meaningful. Two clusters appearing close together does not mean they are globally similar. The inter-cluster layout changes with perplexity and random seed. - Do not use t-SNE for feature extraction. The mapping is not stable and cannot be applied to new data points without refitting. Use PCA or UMAP if you need features. - t-SNE scales poorly: O(n²) time and memory in the naive implementation, O(n log n) with the Barnes-Hut approximation.
When to use: - Exploratory visualization of high-dimensional data to assess whether meaningful cluster structure exists - Sanity-checking embeddings (e.g., visualizing word embeddings, BERT representations) - Communicating data structure to stakeholders who need an intuitive picture
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

# t-SNE is slow — subsample large datasets
max_samples = 5000
if len(X_scaled) > max_samples:
    idx = np.random.choice(len(X_scaled), max_samples, replace=False)
    X_viz = X_scaled[idx]
    y_viz = y[idx]  # labels for coloring (if available)
else:
    X_viz, y_viz = X_scaled, y

# First reduce with PCA to 50 dims — speeds up t-SNE significantly
X_pca50 = PCA(n_components=50, random_state=42).fit_transform(X_viz)

tsne = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30, n_iter=1000,
            random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
X_tsne = tsne.fit_transform(X_pca50)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
scatter = plt.scatter(X_tsne[:, 0], X_tsne[:, 1], c=y_viz,
                      cmap='tab10', alpha=0.6, s=5)
plt.colorbar(scatter); plt.title('t-SNE Visualization'); plt.show()

⚠️ Common Mistake: Interpreting cluster sizes and distances in a t-SNE plot as meaningful. They are not. The only interpretable information is local neighborhood structure — points that cluster together were likely nearby in the original space.




5.2.3 UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection)
Plain-English definition: A non-linear dimensionality reduction technique grounded in topological data analysis that is faster than t-SNE, preserves more global structure, and can be used both for visualization and feature extraction.
How it works: UMAP constructs a fuzzy topological representation of the high-dimensional data (modeling the manifold the data lies on) and optimizes a low-dimensional representation to have a similar fuzzy topology. The mathematical grounding in category theory and Riemannian geometry makes UMAP more principled than t-SNE. In practice, the key differences are:

Speed: UMAP is 5-20× faster than t-SNE on the same data
Scalability: UMAP can handle millions of points; t-SNE cannot
Global structure: UMAP better preserves the relative positions of clusters (inter-cluster distances are more meaningful, though still not perfectly faithful)
Supervised UMAP: You can provide partial labels to guide the embedding — useful when you have some labeled data and want the low-dimensional space to respect class structure

When to use UMAP over t-SNE: - Large datasets (>10K points) - You need a reusable transformation (UMAP can transform new data points with transform()) - Feature engineering: use UMAP as a non-linear feature extractor in a preprocessing pipeline - You care about global structure as well as local clusters
import umap

# UMAP for visualization
reducer = umap.UMAP(n_components=2, n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1,
                    random_state=42)
X_umap = reducer.fit_transform(X_scaled)

# UMAP for feature extraction (can be used on new data)
reducer_features = umap.UMAP(n_components=10, n_neighbors=30,
                               min_dist=0.0, random_state=42)
reducer_features.fit(X_train_scaled)
X_train_umap = reducer_features.transform(X_train_scaled)
X_test_umap = reducer_features.transform(X_test_scaled)  # reusable!

💡 Senior Tip: n_neighbors controls the balance between local and global structure. Small values (5-15) emphasize local neighborhoods; large values (50-200) capture more global topology. min_dist controls cluster compactness in the embedding — 0.0 creates tightly packed clusters useful for discrete cluster analysis; 0.1-0.5 preserves more continuous structure.

title: 4  Unsupervised Learning, Evaluation Metrics & Feature Engineering
text:
6.1 Classification Metrics

6.1.1 The Confusion Matrix Foundation
Every classification metric derives from the confusion matrix. For a binary classifier:




Predicted Positive
Predicted Negative




Actually Positive
True Positive (TP)
False Negative (FN)


Actually Negative
False Positive (FP)
True Negative (TN)



The four cells tell you everything about classifier behavior. The question is which combination of these cells matters for your use case.



6.1.2 Accuracy
\(\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN}\)
Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that are correct. It is the most intuitive metric and the most commonly misused one. On a balanced dataset (equal class distribution), accuracy is a reasonable first-pass metric. On an imbalanced dataset, it is nearly meaningless.
The 99% accuracy trap: Imagine a fraud detection model where 1% of transactions are fraudulent. A model that predicts “not fraud” for every single transaction achieves 99% accuracy — and catches exactly zero fraudulent transactions. The model is useless by its intended purpose, but accuracy scores it perfectly. This is the most important metric intuition to internalize before any interview.






Warning



When to avoid accuracy: Any dataset where class frequencies differ by more than 2:1. In practice, churn prediction (5-20% churn), fraud detection (0.1-2%), medical diagnosis (rare disease prevalence), and anomaly detection all require metrics beyond accuracy.





6.1.3 Precision, Recall, and F1
Precision = \(\frac{TP}{TP + FP}\) — of everything the model labeled positive, what fraction was actually positive? A precision-optimized model is cautious: it only fires when confident, accepting that it will miss some real positives.
Recall = \(\frac{TP}{TP + FN}\) — of everything that was actually positive, what fraction did the model catch? A recall-optimized model casts a wide net: it catches most true positives, accepting that it will also flag many false positives.
The tension between precision and recall is fundamental: as you lower the classification threshold to catch more true positives (increasing recall), you will inevitably flag more false positives (decreasing precision). This tradeoff cannot be escaped — it can only be managed by choosing the right operating point.
When each matters: - Precision critical: Spam filtering (flagging a legitimate email as spam is costly), content moderation (removing real user content), ad targeting (wasting budget on non-converting impressions) - Recall critical: Cancer screening (missing a real cancer case is catastrophic), fraud detection (missing fraud costs money), safety systems (missing a dangerous event has severe consequences)
F1 score = \(\frac{2 \cdot \text{Precision} \cdot \text{Recall}}{\text{Precision} + \text{Recall}}\) — the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is higher when both are high and punishes extreme imbalances between the two. F-beta generalizes this: \(F_\beta = (1+\beta^2) \cdot \frac{P \cdot R}{\beta^2 P + R}\) — a \(\beta > 1\) weights recall higher than precision.

⚠️ Common Mistake: Averaging F1 across classes incorrectly. macro average treats all classes equally regardless of support (may be misleading if class sizes are very unequal). weighted average weights by class support. micro average computes globally from TP/FP/FN totals. Always specify which averaging strategy and why.




6.1.4 ROC-AUC
The Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve plots True Positive Rate (recall) on the y-axis vs. False Positive Rate (\(FP / (FP + TN)\)) on the x-axis at every possible classification threshold. A perfect classifier achieves (0, 1) — TPR=1, FPR=0 at some threshold. A random classifier traces the diagonal line TPR=FPR.
AUC (Area Under the ROC Curve) summarizes the entire curve in one number: - AUC = 0.5: random classifier (useless) - AUC = 0.7: acceptable for many problems - AUC = 0.85: good discrimination - AUC = 0.95+: excellent; question whether data leakage is inflating it - AUC = 1.0: perfect discrimination (almost certainly leakage in production data)
A useful probabilistic interpretation: AUC is the probability that the classifier assigns a higher score to a randomly chosen positive example than to a randomly chosen negative example.
Threshold independence is the key advantage of ROC-AUC: it evaluates the model’s discriminative ability across all thresholds simultaneously. This makes it useful for comparing classifiers before committing to an operating threshold.






Warning



When ROC-AUC misleads: On highly imbalanced datasets, the large number of true negatives dominates the FPR axis. The ROC curve can look excellent (high AUC) even when precision is disastrous at the operating threshold. Example: a model with AUC=0.95 on a 1% positive class might have precision of 3% at the operating threshold — it fires 33× more often than necessary.





6.1.5 Precision-Recall Curve
The Precision-Recall (PR) curve plots precision on the y-axis vs. recall on the x-axis at every threshold. It focuses entirely on the positive class and is the correct diagnostic tool for imbalanced classification problems.
AUPRC (Area Under the PR Curve): A random classifier on a dataset with p% positives achieves an AUPRC of p (the baseline). Models must substantially exceed this to be useful. An AUPRC of 0.5 on a 1% positive class is excellent; on a 50-50 balanced class, 0.5 AUPRC is equivalent to random guessing.
Use the PR curve when: - Positive class prevalence is low (fraud, disease, churn in healthy user bases) - False positive costs are high and you need to understand the precision-recall tradeoff explicitly - You are communicating model performance to a business audience that cares about “when we flag something, how often are we right?” (precision) and “how many of the real events do we catch?” (recall)
from sklearn.metrics import (
    classification_report, roc_auc_score, average_precision_score,
    RocCurveDisplay, PrecisionRecallDisplay, confusion_matrix
)
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Assumes binary classifier with predict_proba support
y_prob = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
y_pred = model.predict(X_test)

# Confusion matrix
cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, y_pred)
print("Confusion Matrix:\n", cm)

# Classification report (precision, recall, F1 per class)
print(classification_report(y_test, y_pred, target_names=['Negative', 'Positive']))

# ROC-AUC
roc_auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, y_prob)
print(f"ROC-AUC: {roc_auc:.4f}")

# Average precision (AUPRC)
avg_precision = average_precision_score(y_test, y_prob)
print(f"Average Precision (AUPRC): {avg_precision:.4f}")
print(f"Baseline AUPRC (random): {y_test.mean():.4f}")

# Plot both curves side by side
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
RocCurveDisplay.from_predictions(y_test, y_prob, ax=ax1)
ax1.set_title(f'ROC Curve (AUC={roc_auc:.3f})')
PrecisionRecallDisplay.from_predictions(y_test, y_prob, ax=ax2)
ax2.set_title(f'PR Curve (AUPRC={avg_precision:.3f})')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()



6.1.6 Cohen’s Kappa and MCC
For severely imbalanced datasets, neither accuracy nor F1 captures the full picture. Two metrics that account for chance-level performance are useful here.
Cohen’s Kappa measures inter-rater agreement, corrected for chance: \(\kappa = \frac{p_o - p_e}{1 - p_e}\) where \(p_o\) is observed accuracy and \(p_e\) is expected accuracy from a random classifier with the same marginal distributions. A kappa of 0 means no better than chance; 1.0 means perfect agreement.
Matthews Correlation Coefficient (MCC) is often considered the most informative single metric for imbalanced binary classification: \(MCC = \frac{TP \cdot TN - FP \cdot FN}{\sqrt{(TP+FP)(TP+FN)(TN+FP)(TN+FN)}}\). MCC is the correlation coefficient between actual and predicted binary labels. It ranges from -1 (perfect inverse prediction) to 0 (random) to +1 (perfect). Unlike F1, MCC accounts for all four cells of the confusion matrix and is high only when the classifier performs well on both classes.

💡 Senior Tip: In ML research and competition, MCC is increasingly preferred as the primary metric for binary classification with class imbalance, precisely because it cannot be gamed by a degenerate classifier that always predicts the majority class.

title: 4  Unsupervised Learning, Evaluation Metrics & Feature Engineering
text:
6.2 Regression Metrics

6.2.1 MAE, MSE, RMSE, MAPE
Mean Absolute Error (MAE) = \(\frac{1}{n}\sum|y_i - \hat{y}_i|\) — average absolute deviation from the true value. Interpretable in the original units. Less sensitive to outliers than MSE because it does not square the error.
Mean Squared Error (MSE) = \(\frac{1}{n}\sum(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2\) — penalizes large errors disproportionately (squaring amplifies outlier impact). Used in optimization because it is differentiable everywhere. Loss function for many regression models.
Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) = \(\sqrt{MSE}\) — same units as the target variable, making it more interpretable than MSE. Still penalizes large errors more than MAE. The most commonly reported regression metric.
Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) = \(\frac{100}{n}\sum\left|\frac{y_i - \hat{y}_i}{y_i}\right|\) — expresses error as a percentage of the true value. Scale-independent, allowing comparison across datasets with different magnitudes. Critical flaw: undefined when \(y_i = 0\), and asymmetric (overestimation and underestimation of the same magnitude produce different MAPE values). Use with caution.

Interpretable units
Scale-independent
Use when

Yes
No

No

Yes
Comparing across scales; never use with zero targets






6.2.2 R² and Adjusted R²
R² (coefficient of determination) = \(1 - \frac{SS_{res}}{SS_{tot}}\) — the proportion of variance in the target variable that is explained by the model. A model that always predicts the mean achieves R²=0; a perfect model achieves R²=1. R² can be negative if the model is worse than just predicting the mean.
Adjusted R² penalizes model complexity: \(\bar{R}^2 = 1 - (1-R^2)\frac{n-1}{n-p-1}\) where p is the number of predictors. R² always increases (or stays the same) as you add predictors, even if those predictors are pure noise. Adjusted R² decreases when added predictors do not improve fit enough to justify the added complexity. Use adjusted R² whenever comparing models with different numbers of features.






Warning



Common Mistake: Reporting only R² without domain context. An R² of 0.85 sounds excellent, but in financial price prediction it may reflect a near-random model that happens to track the mean trend. In demand forecasting, a well-calibrated MAE matters more than R². Always pair R² with an absolute error metric.
